A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DGM framework, algorithm and benchmark suite despite the changed title. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.4 report original synthetic-data experiments, timing measurements, simulations and validator analyses, with results in Table 3 and Figures 2–9.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds generator comparisons, noise-injection experiments and a controlled validator study, including results in Appendices B and C.

M1.justification: Column partitioning, separate generators, validator training on authentic and shuffled joins, and iterative acceptance and reshuffling remain unchanged. TabDiff supplies another instance of the existing interchangeable-generator design. The expanded implementation discussion does not establish a revised algorithm.

E1.justification: The eight benchmark datasets and their tasks remain unchanged in Table 1. v2 adds noisy-input scenarios in Appendix B and a controlled two-variable example with ground-truth marginal inputs in Appendix C.2, providing limited additional synthetic test conditions.

E2.justification: Table 3 and Figure 8 expand the mixed-model comparison to include TabDiff, ARF, TVAE, CTGAN, ADS-GAN and TabDDPM. CTGAN appeared elsewhere in v1 but was absent from this comparison. Appendix B additionally evaluates Gaussian noise, random replacement and column-wise shuffling as alternatives to partitioning.

E3.justification: New protocols include three perturbation schemes at five strengths and a 250-sample controlled experiment using ground-truth marginal samples to isolate validator effects (Appendices B and C.2). The original benchmark splits remain unchanged. Table 3 also relabels accuracy differences as F1 differences, although the appendix still describes accuracy; the PDFs do not establish whether this involved recomputation.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds sensitivity comparisons testing whether ordinary noise injection reproduces partitioning's effects. Appendix C.2 adds a controlled analysis of distributional distortion caused by unoptimized versus optimized validators. The earlier correlation, validator-choice, calibration and threshold analyses are retained, with much of v1 Section 4.4 moved into Appendix C.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly states that random seeds were left unlocked and specifies ten repetitions for Table 3. The table newly marks statistically indistinguishable results using 95% confidence intervals. Existing standard-deviation and standard-error reporting largely persists; these disclosures do not establish increased run counts.

E6.justification: Table 3 expands from 12 to 25 result rows, while Figures 7–8 add TabDiff mixtures and broader baseline results. Eleven retained table rows preserve their numbers; the DPGAN–synthpop row changes, including epsilon risk from 0.048(7) to 0.14(3). New noise and validator-distortion findings appear in Figures 10 and 13. The correlation study replaces its PCA panel with AUROC results.

T1.justification: The framework definitions and computational-scaling arguments are retained across the corresponding sections. There are no new substantive assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations. The added noise formulas specify experimental perturbations.

C1.justification: The abstract qualifies the earlier broad privacy benefit as an observed empirical improvement and explicitly claims competitive downstream accuracy and AUROC for mixed-model synthesis. Partitioned generation, computational feasibility and mixed-model synthesis remain the central contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix B introduces substantial interpretation of partitioning as information fragmentation, explains the non-equivalence of noise-strength parameters, and limits the comparison to random concatenation rather than the complete framework. v2 also develops requirements for end-to-end privacy accounting and discusses realistic adversarial applicability. The earlier warnings about non-private validators, partition-aware attacks and selection bias remain.

D1.justification: Appendices A.2 and C.2 newly disclose a 100-iteration limit, typical fourfold oversampling, and typical random-forest settings of 5–20 estimators and depth 10–15. These are additional details rather than established setting changes. Conversely, v2 removes the hardware specifications and dataset-license column. The repository and dataset links were already supplied in v1.

R1.justification: v2 adds contemporary generator and benchmark references, alongside foundational differential-privacy and private-covariance work. It explicitly acknowledges prior partitioning-related efficiency benefits. The established positioning relative to conditional generation, federated learning and record linkage remains largely intact.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and background are revised, and the experimental narrative gains an extensive roadmap and more descriptive subsections. Implementation details move to Appendix A, validator analyses to Appendix C, and metric explanations to Appendix D. The conclusion becomes a discussion, with additional impact and materials statements.

P2.justification: v2 adds validator and noise diagrams, new comparison plots and the distribution-distortion visualization. Table 3 is expanded and reformatted from landscape to portrait with metric groupings and significance styling. Existing plots gain revised labels and directional arrows; the validator comparison changes from a grid to vertically stacked panels.

improvement.justification: The broader contemporary-baseline comparisons substantially strengthen the previously narrow evidence for mixed-model utility–privacy tradeoffs. The controlled experiment in Figure 13 isolates an important validator failure mechanism, while clearer empirical-privacy qualifications improve claim precision. These gains outweigh the loss of hardware and license details. Accuracy/F1 terminology remains inconsistent, and the added noise comparison is explicitly inconclusive, but neither limitation negates the substantial improvement in empirical support and diagnostic depth.
